opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what's actually holding agents back right now. When you look at why an agent fails on a real task, especially a long one, it's usually not because it needed a teammate. It's because it lost track of something: what it already tried, why it made a decision an hour ago, what the user told it last week. Each session starts close to from scratch. So the agent keeps paying the same costs, and it doesn't really get better with experience the way a person does on the job.

Collaboration is exciting, and I'm not saying it doesn't matter. But a lot of multi-agent setups today are working around limits of a single agent, like limited context. You split the work up because one agent can't hold it all. And then you've created a new problem, because the agents have to communicate and share state, and that's lossy and expensive. In a sense, collaboration is itself a memory problem. If two agents need to coordinate, they need a shared, reliable record of what's been done and what's known. If you don't solve that, adding more agents can multiply the confusion rather than the capability.

There's also a compounding argument. Better memory makes every agent better, on every task, and the improvement accumulates over time, because each thing the agent learns stays useful later. Adding a second agent gives you more throughput, maybe, but if both are forgetful, you just have two forgetful agents.

And memory isn't just storing more. Storage is cheap, and we can log everything. The hard part is deciding what's worth keeping, how to organize it, when to update or throw something out, and how to retrieve the right thing at the right moment. That's a really deep research problem, and it's closer to the core of intelligence.

So I'd say get the individual agent to accumulate knowledge and learn from experience first. Then collaboration gets much easier, and much more valuable, because you're building a team out of members who actually remember and improve.

r001.rationale: The response says agents have limited context and lose track of information, but does not address whether unlimited context would still fail to ensure reliable memory.

r002.rationale: It connects better memory with retaining what an agent learns from experience, improving across tasks over time rather than starting from scratch.

r003.rationale: It says multi-agent setups divide work to work around a single agent’s limited context and inability to hold everything.

r004.rationale: The response does not distinguish a single user-facing assistant from backend parallelization.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss user convenience or the burden of orchestrating multiple agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd actually push back a little on the framing. I don't think it's that memory is strictly more important than collaboration, it's more that I think memory is the bottleneck that has to be solved first, and collaboration kind of inherits whatever problems you have in the individual agent.

Let me explain what I mean. If you look at how people are building agents today, most of them are essentially stateless. You have a very capable model, you give it a long context, maybe you attach some retrieval on top, and that's basically the memory story. And it works okay for short tasks. But the moment you want an agent to work on something over days or weeks, or to actually learn from its own mistakes, you run into this wall where everything it's experienced just gets thrown away or compressed in some ad hoc way. The model itself doesn't change. The weights are frozen. So the "learning" is really just text accumulating in a buffer.

I think that's a fundamental limitation, and it's one where I don't think we even have the right abstractions yet. What should an agent remember? How should it decide what to forget? How do you consolidate many episodes into something more like a skill rather than a transcript? These feel like questions about representation learning, honestly, which is where my own background is, and I think we're still at a pretty early stage.

Now, compare that to multi-agent systems. There's a lot of excitement there, and I understand why. You put several agents together, they debate, they divide up the work, and you get nice demos. But if you look carefully at a lot of those results, the gains are often fairly modest, and sometimes what you're really getting is just more compute, more sampling, more test-time search dressed up as collaboration. And if each individual agent forgets everything and can't improve, then a committee of them has the same problem. You've just multiplied it.

So my view is that if you make a single agent that can genuinely accumulate experience and get better over time, collaboration becomes much more natural and much more valuable on top of that. The reverse isn't true. That's why, when I think about where I'd spend research effort right now, I'd put it on memory.

r001.rationale: It says long context and retrieval are inadequate for work over days or weeks, but does not explain that even unlimited context fails to ensure reliable memory.

r002.rationale: It connects agents’ failure to retain experience with frozen weights and learning reduced to text in a buffer, framing the issue as a limitation on learning over time.

r003.rationale: It argues that multiple agents inherit an individual agent’s memory problems, but does not say task division arises from one agent’s inability to remember everything.

r004.rationale: It does not distinguish a single user-facing assistant from backend parallelization.

r005.rationale: It does not compare the convenience of interacting with one assistant against orchestrating multiple agents.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t necessarily say memory is always more important, but I think it’s a more fundamental limitation right now. If an agent works with you on a long task, it needs to remember what you’ve tried, why something failed, and which decisions you’ve already made. Otherwise, you spend a lot of time giving it the same context again.

Adding more agents doesn’t automatically solve that. They still need to share context and keep track of what each other has done, so you can end up adding coordination problems on top of the memory problem.

What I’d like to see is an agent that gets better at helping you over time because it can retain useful experience. And that’s not just storing every interaction. It’s knowing what to keep, when to retrieve it, and when an old piece of information is no longer relevant. If we can do that well, I think it also gives us a stronger foundation for collaboration between agents.

r001.rationale: The response discusses retaining and retrieving useful experience, but does not say that unlimited context still cannot guarantee reliable memory.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent improving over time, but does not connect preventing forgetting to continual learning.

r003.rationale: It says adding agents does not automatically solve memory problems, but does not argue that task division arises because one agent cannot remember everything.

r004.rationale: The response does not distinguish a single user-facing assistant from backend parallelization.

r005.rationale: It does not judge using one personal assistant as more convenient than orchestrating multiple agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say memory is always more important, but I think it’s a more fundamental bottleneck right now. If you want an agent to work with you over a long period, it needs to remember what you’ve done together, what your preferences are, and which approaches have already failed. Otherwise, you spend a lot of time giving it the same context again.

Having multiple agents collaborate can be useful, especially when a task can be divided into independent pieces. But adding more agents doesn’t automatically solve that continuity problem. They still need to preserve useful information and share the right context.

So I would prioritize making one agent learn effectively from its experience. And memory here isn’t just storing everything—it’s deciding what to keep, what to retrieve, and when to update it. If we get that right, it should also make collaboration between agents much more effective.
